newsitem.title: UK: Investors take a shine to base metals, coffee.
newsitem.headline: Investors take a shine to base metals, coffee.

text.p: A burst of speculator buying boosted prices for several base metals led by copper on Wednesday.

A New Year rebound in activity in the commodity sector also extended to coffee where prices have jumped on a prospect of a lower-than-expected Brazil crop. A rally in oil paused and gold extended its decline. Investment fund money was attracted to the London Metal Exchange's (LME) industrial metals complex by a strong performance from the flagship copper contract despite bearish news on Tuesday.
Analysts of technical charts also said they saw encouraging signs for buyers of metals.

Three months delivery copper on the LME raced up $30 early Wednesday to $2,252 a tonne as traders focused on supply tightness in Europe and ignored the largest single rise, of 11,475 tonnes, in the LME warehouse copper stocks for a year.
Most of that metal was delivered into Singapore warehouses which, traders claimed, would do nothing to alleviate a shortage in European markets.

"Base metals prices frequently enjoy a bout of strength across the turn of the year and there is further evidence that this could be coming through now," said Investment Research of Cambridge in a market report.
"Copper prices have picked up strongly and look likely to head for their November high at $2,313," they added.
Aluminium prices enjoyed a $21 rise to $1,581 a tonne, the highest for seven months, as traders and analysts remained excited about consumption prospects for the metal during 1997.

Nickel extended by $100 its recent surge higher as traders reckoned the worst of the slump in demand from an overstocked stainless steel industry, which accounts for 60 percent of nickel offtake, was over.
It reached $7,250 a tonne after a recent fall below $6,400.
In a market comment brokers Rudolf Wolff put a target of $1,650 for aluminium and $7,500 for nickel.
The coffee market was still absorbing the impact of the possibility of a lower than expected 1997/98 crop from the world's largest producer Brazil.
On Tuesday an official at Brazil's Industry and Commerce Ministry said it was working with a preliminary range of between 18.5 and 19.5 million 60 kg bags.
This compared with trade estimates of upto 24 million bags although local co-operative forecasts have been much lower.
The benchmark March delivery coffee contract on the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) reached $1,302, a rise of $75 from Tuesday.
February Brent crude oil on the International Petroleum Exchange dropped 14 cents after American Petroleum Institute data showed a rise in distillate stocks in the U.S.
But traders reckoned that with the cold spell continuing in Europe any price fall would be restricted.

Gold's brief rally on Tuesday only served to bring more selling into the market and the spot bullion price neared its lowest since October 1993 when it was fixed in London at $355.80 on Wednesday morning.

Dealers said a report from an authoritative research group, Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS), that gold sales from the official sector (central banks) had accelerated in the second half of 1996 was a major factor weakening the price.
